title: When Machines Talk
text:
Preface
I downloaded a dataset with a practical goal in mind: learn what an event log can tell about the machine that generated it.
The log is from Galdi filling machines — five machines, two years, 429,000 rows of real production data — hosted on Kaggle.
I expected to spend a few hours max on it. That was several weeks ago…
Basic exploratory analysis first. Each answer opened the next question, and the next one was always more interesting than the last. A structure emerged, patterns appeared. And then came a different question: can we formalize this? Turn the observations into a grammar — a systematic language to communicate with machines?
These seven episodes trace the path from raw data to a working language.

 Image courtesy of jcomp, on Freepik

Stack: R, tidyverse, Quarto Dataset: Packaging Industry Anomaly Detection — Diego Tosato et al., Galdi

title: Episode 1 — First Read
text:
What a row looks like
132 alarm codes. No dictionary. We’ll have to figure them out.
First look at the data. Here’s what a few rows look like:
Each row is a time interval — a continuous period during which the machine was in a given state. The type column says what was happening, alarm gives the alarm code (if any), and speed is recorded alongside.
Five machines, but they didn’t all start at the same time — and they didn’t start from zero.
s_2 and s_3 show up later — not all machines were active from the start.
Each row is an interval — a continuous period in a given state. The end of one is the start of the next. No gaps. No overlaps.

The five state types already point towards performance analysis. But one number stands out.
performance_loss: 28% of all intervals. The machines are running — but not at full speed. No breakdown. No alarm. And yet it’s the second most frequent state in the log.

title: Episode 1 — First Read
text:
Why this distinction matters





A machine that runs all day with no downtime but spends half its time below full speed looks healthy if we only count stoppages. performance_loss captures the gap — and it’s large.

title: Episode 1 — First Read
text:
The codes I can’t read
Every unplanned downtime interval carries an alarm code. There are 133 distinct codes in this log — from A_000 to A_132. A_000 seems to mean ‘normal operation’. The other 132 appear during stoppages.
I found no public dictionary to translate these codes into fault descriptions.
132 alarm codes, no Rosetta Stone. Just repeated patterns, frequencies, co-occurrences — and no translation key. We’ll have to figure out the meaning from behaviour. That’s what the following episodes do.

The values are large and grow from row to row — they’re cumulative counters, not per-interval counts. To get what happened during an interval, we need the difference with the previous row (delta_pi, delta_po).
If these counters are reliable, they should grow steadily over time — a straight line going up.





Cumulative counters pi (packages in) and po (packages out) over two years, by machine. A well-behaved counter is a straight line going up.




Ouch… s_1 and s_3 are clean — steady growth, pi and po tracking each other. The rest is less reassuring. s_2 shows a spike to 300 million then drops back to near zero. s_4 oscillates instead of growing — the counter goes down, which a cumulative counter shouldn’t do. s_5 has a clean reset to zero mid-series.
These counters can’t be trusted at interval level. And on some machines, not even at daily level.






What this rules out





The reject rate calculated from delta_po − delta_pi per interval measures sensor behaviour, not production quality. On short windows, the signal is drowned in noise. For an interpretable figure, aggregating over at least a full day is necessary.

title: Episode 1 — First Read
section: Five machines — but not a fleet
text:
Five machines — but not a fleet
We’d expect these five machines to be of the same type and do the same work. The speed setpoints say otherwise.





Speed setpoint distribution by machine (share of active time per 500 pkg/h bin, excluding start/stop).




The speed regimes don’t overlap. Some machines run at high throughput; others at much lower setpoints. They don’t run at the same speed.
And their co-activity confirms the same thing:





Fraction of total time where both machines are simultaneously in production. Dark = often together; light = rarely together.










How to read this matrix





Each cell shows the fraction of total time where both machines are simultaneously in production (5-minute grid over the full history). A score near zero means they almost never run together — they alternate. A high score means they operate in parallel.



Some pairs run together. Others almost never do. Comparing their performance as if they were doing the same job would give us numbers that mean nothing.

title: Episode 1 — First Read
text:
What the machines are hiding
No diagnosis yet. But we now have a map of what we don’t know.
133 alarm codes with no dictionary. A state — performance_loss — that slips through standard reporting. Counters that drift. Five machines that aren’t in the same league.

title: Episode 1 — First Read
text:
What to do about it
These five machines can’t be pooled. Different speed regimes, different histories, different co-activity patterns. Aggregating them would give us averages that describe none of them.
The counters are unreliable at interval level. pi and po are useful over full days or longer. Below that, they measure noise.
performance_loss matters. It accounts for 28% of intervals. If we only look at downtimes, we miss a quarter of what’s going on.

Next: Let’s compute OEE. The results are not what the availability numbers would suggest.

title: Episode 2 — OEE: when availability lies
text:
What OEE measures here
Five machines. One indicator. And one that shows 94% availability for a 44% OEE.
A single OEE value tells almost nothing. It’s the breakdown that reveals where the time goes — and what the headline number hides.
OEE will be computed without the quality component — the pi/po counters aren’t reliable enough, as we saw in Episode 1.
crumbs: 2  Episode 2 — OEE: when availability lies

title: Episode 2 — OEE: when availability lies
text:
Method note — Time-based OEE





OEE = Availability × Performance

Availability = (open time − downtime) / open time
Performance = production time / (production + performance_loss + idle)

A time-based variant, suited to logs where volume counters are absent or unreliable.

title: Episode 2 — OEE: when availability lies
text:
The s_4 paradox
s_4 is the second most reliable machine in the group: 94% availability. It rarely stops. And yet its OEE is 44%.





Time breakdown for s_4 (open time only). Performance loss accounts for a quarter of available time.




Over two years, s_4 spent roughly 1,540 hours in performance_loss — a quarter of its open time. The machine was running. No alarm was triggered. But it was barely producing.
performance_loss is the least visible state: no alarm, no logged stoppage, just a speed below target.

The time dimension — s_1 under the lens
s_1 is the reference machine: two full years of data, best OEE in the group. Let’s see how its OEE evolves month by month.





Monthly OEE for s_1. The dashed red line is the two-year average. Automatic changepoint detection finds no structural break — the machine is stable.










Method note — Changepoint detection





Automatically detects periods where the average OEE is stable — without setting the number of breaks in advance. Reveals whether a machine has degraded, improved, or has been running on the same plateau for months.

title: Episode 2 — OEE: when availability lies
text:
What the machines are hiding
Performance, not availability, is the real problem. All five machines have availability above 86%. Yet four out of five have an OEE below 55%. The gap is in performance_loss and idle — not in breakdowns.
s_4 doesn’t break down — it runs on empty. 94% availability, 1,540 hours of performance_loss over two years. The machine runs, no alarm fires, but it barely produces. The log alone doesn’t tell us why.
s_1 has been on a plateau for two years. No visible progressive degradation. Its worst month stays within the regime envelope.
crumbs: 2  Episode 2 — OEE: when availability lies

title: Episode 2 — OEE: when availability lies
text:
What to do about it
The alarms behind these losses are the next target. Which codes cost the most time? The next episode finds out.
Some questions are beyond this log. performance_loss on s_4 and idle time on several machines are major losses — but the log doesn’t carry enough context to explain them. The rest of this book focuses on what the data can answer: downtime patterns, alarm behaviour, and predictability.

Next: 132 alarm codes. Which ones hurt?

title: Episode 3 — Which alarms hurt
text:
One fingerprint per machine





Alarm fingerprint by machine. Each cell shows total time lost (hours) for that machine × alarm pair. Values below 5h are not labelled.










Method note — Alarm fingerprint





A nearly empty column = a problem specific to one machine. A uniformly filled column = a problem shared across machines. Separates local faults from systemic ones at a glance.

title: Episode 3 — Which alarms hurt
text:
How do they occur?
We know which alarms cost the most and where they hit. But do they strike regularly?





Occurrence pattern of the top 3 alarms by time lost. Each dot = one event. Dense horizontal bands = burst days.




Same Pareto ranking, completely different behaviours. s_1 / A_065 comes in dense bursts — the machine cycles between failure and restart all day long. s_3 / A_006 only appears when the machine is active (s_3 was offline until late 2020) — but once active, it’s present consistently. s_5 / A_101 is spread evenly across active days, with gaps matching periods when the machine was down.

title: Episode 3 — Which alarms hurt
text:
What the machines are hiding
A Pareto is not enough. The same alarm can be a daily burst on one machine and a constant background on another.
Each machine has its own alarm signature. Some alarms are local. Others are shared. The fingerprint separates the two.
The worst alarms are stable. The top codes in the Pareto have been there since the beginning — no sudden change, no improvement. They’re structural.

title: Episode 3 — Which alarms hurt
text:
What to do about it
We’ve mapped the alarms — how much they cost, where they hit, and how they behave. The next question is whether there are patterns in when they happen.

Next: what happens just before a failure?

title: Episode 4 — What happens before a failure
text:
Do states predict downtimes?
Do failures leave traces in the log? We look at what happens before, during, and between them.
So far we’ve looked at each state on its own — how much time it costs, where it hits, how it behaves.
But a downtime doesn’t appear out of thin air. Is there something before it?
First question: what state does a machine come from when it enters a downtime?
State immediately before a downtime. 99% come straight from production — no visible slow-down beforehand.
99% of downtimes come straight from production. No slow degradation visible at the state level — the machine produces, then stops. The state type alone doesn’t predict what’s coming.
crumbs: 4  Episode 4 — What happens before a failure

title: Episode 4 — What happens before a failure
text:
Do consecutive alarm pairs repeat?





Top 20 consecutive alarm pairs (all machines), by frequency.










Method note — Alarm bigrams





Consecutive alarm pairs on the same machine, same day. Dominant bigrams reveal repetitive sequences — often the same problem recurring until it’s resolved.



The dominant pairs are an alarm followed by itself — the same code firing repeatedly until resolved.
crumbs: 4  Episode 4 — What happens before a failure

title: Episode 4 — What happens before a failure
text:
Zooming out: the process map
We’ve been looking at individual transitions and alarm pairs. Stepping back: what does the overall flow between states look like?















Method note — Process map





Aggregates all state transitions across sessions. Arc thickness reflects probability. Shows dominant flows and loops at a glance.



The dominant cycle is visible: production ↔︎ downtime, with perf. loss as a transition state (especially after idle — the startup ramp-up). But this pattern is the same for every machine. It doesn’t tell us which failure is coming or when.
crumbs: 4  Episode 4 — What happens before a failure

title: Episode 4 — What happens before a failure
text:
What the machines are hiding
Do failures leave traces? At the state level, no — 99% come straight from production. At the alarm level, the same codes repeat in cycles. The trace is in the pattern, not in the state.
crumbs: 4  Episode 4 — What happens before a failure

title: Episode 4 — What happens before a failure
text:
What to do about it
The same alarm code can behave very differently — dense bursts one day, nothing the next. The Pareto sees the total. The patterns tell a different story.

Next: we look for the events that don’t fit any pattern — anomalies in duration and timing.
crumbs: 4  Episode 4 — What happens before a failure

title: Episode 5 — The outliers
text:
Unusually long stops
Averages hide extremes. This episode looks for the events that don’t fit.
So far we’ve ranked alarms, mapped them to machines, and looked at sequences. All of that works on aggregates — totals, averages, distributions. But a stop that lasts ten times longer than usual for the same alarm code doesn’t move the average much. It doesn’t trigger a special alert. It’s just there, in the data, with a date and a code.
Two approaches to find it.
Same alarm, same machine. 30 seconds one day, 45 minutes the next. The red dots below are the statistically unusual ones — not necessarily the longest in absolute terms, but the farthest from the history of that alarm on that machine.
Duration distribution for the 8 most active alarm codes. Red dots = events unusually long for their alarm on their machine.
The red dots are where something different happened. Same alarm code, but a duration far outside the norm for that machine. Some red dots appear inside the violin because the violin mixes all machines — the event is unusual for its machine even if it looks normal for the group.

title: Episode 5 — The outliers
text:
Method note — Duration anomalies





Compares each stop to the historical distribution of the same alarm on the same machine. Threshold: 3 standard deviations above the mean. Finds stops that are unusually long for their alarm — even if their absolute duration is moderate.

title: Episode 5 — The outliers
text:
Are there high-risk hours?
Machines don’t fail randomly throughout the day. Operational routines — whatever they are — create hourly patterns.





Average downtime rate by hour of day, per machine. Peaks reveal structurally loaded hours.




Red bars mark the hours with the highest downtime rate for each machine. Each machine has its own rhythm. s_1 and s_2 peak in the early morning. s_3 peaks in the afternoon (13–17h). s_4 has an isolated spike at 2am. s_5 shows mild peaks mid-morning and evening.






Method note — Hourly profile





Computes the average downtime rate per hour over two years. Reveals structurally loaded hours — and whether machines share the same daily rhythm or not.

title: Episode 5 — The outliers
text:
What the machines are hiding
Every alarm has outliers. The same code can last 6 seconds or 15 hours. Duration is not predictable from the alarm code alone.
Each machine has its own daily rhythm. Some peak in the morning, others in the afternoon. Without the shift schedule we can’t explain why — but the profiles are distinct.

title: Episode 5 — The outliers
text:
What to do about it
The data shows the what — not the why. Alarm durations are unpredictable, and each machine has its own daily rhythm. Explaining these patterns would require context the log doesn’t carry — shift schedules, operator actions, maintenance history.

Next: we’ve been looking at alarms separately — rankings, patterns, anomalies. What happens when we look at how they relate to each other?

title: Episode 6 — The Rosetta Stone
text:
132 codes, seen together
132 alarm codes. No dictionary. But the data knows how to read them.
Five episodes of investigation — the dataset, OEE, alarm rankings, sequences, anomalies. Each episode added a piece. But we were always looking at alarms separately.
What if we looked at all of them at once?
Which alarms tend to show up on the same days, on the same machines? A Principal Component Analysis (PCA) looks at alarm co-occurrences and finds the main directions that separate the machines.
Machine similarity based on alarm profiles. 100% = same alarms, 0% = completely different.
s_1 and s_4 have 0% similarity — completely different alarm profiles. s_3 and s_5 are 85% similar. These are not five copies of the same machine.

title: Episode 6 — The Rosetta Stone
text:
Method note — PCA on alarm co-occurrences





For each day and machine, we record which alarms were present (yes/no). PCA finds the directions in this data that best separate the machines. The similarity score measures how much two machines share the same alarm behaviour — 100% means identical profiles, 0% means nothing in common.

title: Episode 6 — The Rosetta Stone
text:
The pieces fall into place
This changes how we read everything that came before.
Episode 1 said these five machines weren’t a fleet — different speeds, different histories. The PCA confirms it at the alarm level: each machine has its own failure family. Not the same breakdowns happening to five copies of the same equipment.
Episode 2 showed the s_4 paradox — 94% availability, 44% OEE. The PCA shows that s_4 has its own alarm family — a group of codes that fire together.
Episode 3 showed A_065 bursting in dense daily cycles on s_1. The PCA confirms it’s not a single alarm — A_065, A_066, A_067, A_068 belong to the same family. A whole subsystem.
Episode 5 showed each machine has its own daily rhythm. Combined with the PCA, it confirms that machines don’t just differ in which alarms they have — they differ in when they happen.

title: Episode 6 — The Rosetta Stone
section: What leads to a long stop?
text:
What leads to a long stop?
Now that we know each machine has its own alarm family, we can look for statistical associations within each machine. A model learns which alarms are most strongly associated with long stops — applied per machine, not globally.

Strongest predictors of long stop

s_2

s_3

When we stop mixing machines, the associations become clear. Each machine has its own set of predictors — different alarms, different combinations.






Method note — Bayesian network per machine





Learns which alarms are most strongly associated with long stops. Applied per machine instead of globally, the noise from other machines disappears and the structural links emerge.

title: Episode 6 — The Rosetta Stone
text:
The escalation path
On s_1, the model identifies a sequence: A_065 typically precedes A_001, which precedes a long stop. We can verify the order directly in the timestamps.
On burst days where both A_065 and A_001 appear, A_065 fires first 72% of the time, with a median lead of 251 minutes before A_001 shows up.
That’s a confirmed sequence — A_065 tends to precede A_001, which precedes the long stop. Turning this into an operational alert would require knowing how much time an operator needs to intervene. The data shows the sequence — the plant defines the action window.

title: Episode 6 — The Rosetta Stone
text:
What predicts a long stop?
Beyond alarm sequences, a broader question: can the machine’s recent behaviour predict a long stop?
On s_1, the strongest predictor is not a specific alarm code — it’s the accumulation of downtime in the last 30 minutes. A machine that has been stopping and restarting repeatedly is more likely to hit a long stop next. The pattern matters more than the individual alarm.
On s_4, no signal was found — the log alone doesn’t carry enough information to predict long stops on every machine.

title: Episode 6 — The Rosetta Stone
text:
The Rosetta Stone
In Episode 1, we had 132 alarm codes and no dictionary. Six episodes later, here’s what we’ve built:

Each machine has its own alarm family. s_1 and s_4 share 0% of their alarm profiles. The codes aren’t random — they group by machine.
Each family has a distinct behaviour. s_1’s family fires in bursts. s_3 and s_5 share similar profiles. Some alarms are common across machines.
The statistical links are machine-specific. On s_1, A_065 precedes A_001, which precedes a long stop. On s_4, it’s a different set entirely. Mixing machines hides these associations.
Alarm sequences have a direction. On s_1, A_065 fires before A_001 72% of the time, with a median 251-minute lead. The sequence is confirmed — making it actionable requires knowing the operator’s response time.
The cost is quantifiable. Eliminating a single alarm family on s_1 would recover 11.1 points of OEE.

That’s the Rosetta Stone: 132 opaque codes, decoded into families, associations, escalation paths, and costs — from behaviour alone, without a dictionary.

title: Episode 6 — The Rosetta Stone
text:
The methodology lesson
We started by looking at everything together — all machines, all alarms. That was necessary: we needed the big picture first. But the real structure only appeared when we separated what needed to be separated.
When we don’t know where to look, we start with the whole. As differences emerge, we isolate them. The PCA told us what to separate. The per-machine analysis told us why.

title: Episode 6 — The Rosetta Stone
text:
What the machines are hiding
The alarms are not 132 independent problems. They organise into families that correspond to machines.
Mixing machines hides the structure. Every analysis becomes sharper when we stop pooling machines that have nothing in common.
The warning signal is in the accumulation, not in a single alarm. On some machines, the pattern of repeated stops in the last 30 minutes predicts a long stop. On others, the log alone isn’t enough.

title: Episode 6 — The Rosetta Stone
text:
What to do about it
Treat each alarm family as a maintenance project, not each alarm code. s_1’s signature alarms (A_065, A_066, A_067…) are a family. Fixing one without addressing the others won’t solve the problem.
Making predictions actionable requires knowing the operator’s response time. The data identifies the sequences. The plant defines how fast someone can act on them.

Next: everything in this book was built with the same set of R functions. Can we turn that into a systematic language — a grammar for asking any machine the same questions?

title: Episode 7 — Behind the scenes
text:
The LEGO principle
Everything in this book was built with the same set of tools.
Six episodes. OEE, alarm rankings, sequences, anomalies, alarm families, escalation paths, costs.
All of it was built with a consistent set of R tools — designed to work on any machine log, not just this one.
I think in LEGO. Each brick does one thing. The bricks snap together. And from the same box, you can build very different things depending on the question.
That’s how these tools are designed. One brick computes an OEE. Another ranks alarms. Another finds alarm families. The six episodes are six different assemblies from the same box of bricks.

title: Episode 7 — Behind the scenes
text:
A language for machine logs
Every question we asked follows the same structure:

What are we measuring? (OEE, alarm duration, similarity…)
Where? (one machine, all machines, one alarm family…)
Over what period? (full dataset, last month, before/after a date…)
Compared to what? (a target, another machine, the machine’s own history…)

That structure is a grammar — a systematic way of asking machines the same questions, regardless of which machine, which plant, which industry. The dataset here is food packaging. The method applies the same to pharma, automotive, electronics — any process where machines produce interval logs.

title: Episode 7 — Behind the scenes
text:

title: Episode 7 — Behind the scenes
text:
You’ve only seen half
The six episodes explored the dataset step by step. The tools behind them now go further. Here are a few examples.
The funnel. 132 alarm codes in the log. The diagnosis layer filters automatically — Pareto, then exclusion of low-impact alarms. On this dataset: 132 → 11 → 4 alarms that concentrate the investigation. Not a catalogue. A shortlist.
Period comparison. The tools can compare two time windows and produce conclusions in plain language:
Not charts. Not numbers. Sentences — written for someone who needs to decide what to do next.
Prediction. On some machines, the accumulation of downtime in the last 30 minutes predicts a long stop better than any individual alarm code. The tools can learn these patterns. On others, the log alone isn’t enough — which is also a result.

title: Episode 7 — Behind the scenes
text:
No AI inside
To be clear: none of this relies on artificial intelligence. The methods are established, documented, and interpretable — no neural network, no black box. Statistics and domain knowledge, formalised into modular tools that snap together.
That said, a natural extension exists: a local language model that translates plain-language questions into the right analysis call. I built and tested the concept — it works. A question goes in — in whatever language — the right analysis comes out. The logic is language-agnostic. And everything stays local — even offline.
But it’s an option, not a dependency. The grammar works without it.

title: Episode 7 — Behind the scenes
text:
Still growing
These tools are still actively developed and tested on real data. They work — but they’re not finished. The toolbox grows with every new question.

title: Episode 7 — Behind the scenes
text:
When machines talk
This started as an exercise on a public dataset. It ended with something I didn’t plan: a language.
Not a programming language — a communication language. A way to listen to what machines say through their logs. To translate their alarms, their patterns, their silences into questions and answers.
The log isn’t just a record of what happened. It’s raw material for decisions — adjust a parameter, schedule an intervention, change a procedure.
That’s what this book is about. Listening.

Arnaud Coqueblin

title: When Machines Talk
text:
What a row looks like
Each row is an interval — a continuous period in a given state. The end of one is the start of the next. No gaps. No overlaps.
%%| fig-cap: "Each row is a continuous interval in one state."
graph LR
  A[sched. downtime] --> B[idle]
  B --> C[production]
  C --> D[downtime]
  D --> E[production]
  style A fill:#e8dcc8,color:#333
  style B fill:#c8c8c8,color:#333
  style C fill:#1d6fa4,color:#fff
  style D fill:#c0392b,color:#fff
  style E fill:#1d6fa4,color:#fff
There are exactly five state types:
df |>
  count(type, sort = TRUE) |>
  mutate(pct = scales::percent(n / sum(n), accuracy = 0.1)) |>
  rename(State = type, Count = n, Share = pct) |>
  kbl() |>
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover"), full_width = FALSE)
The five state types already point towards performance analysis. But one number stands out.
performance_loss: 28% of all intervals. The machines are running — but not at full speed. No breakdown. No alarm. And yet it’s the second most frequent state in the log.






Why this distinction matters





A machine that runs all day with no downtime but spends half its time below full speed looks healthy if we only count stoppages. performance_loss captures the gap — and it’s large.

title: When Machines Talk
text:
The codes I can’t read
Every unplanned downtime interval carries an alarm code. There are 133 distinct codes in this log — from A_000 to A_132. A_000 seems to mean ‘normal operation’. The other 132 appear during stoppages.
I found no public dictionary to translate these codes into fault descriptions.
132 alarm codes, no Rosetta Stone. Just repeated patterns, frequencies, co-occurrences — and no translation key. We’ll have to figure out the meaning from behaviour. That’s what the following episodes do.

title: When Machines Talk
When Machines Talk
section: Five machines — but not a fleet
text:
Five machines — but not a fleet
We’d expect these five machines to be of the same type and do the same work. The speed setpoints say otherwise.
#| fig-cap: "Speed setpoint distribution by machine (share of active time per 500 pkg/h bin, excluding start/stop)."
#| fig-height: 3.5

df |>
  filter(speed > 0) |>
  mutate(speed_bin = round(speed / 500) * 500) |>
  group_by(equipment_ID, speed_bin) |>
  summarise(elapsed_s = sum(elapsed_s), .groups = "drop") |>
  group_by(equipment_ID) |>
  mutate(pct_time = elapsed_s / sum(elapsed_s)) |>
  ungroup() |>
  ggplot(aes(x = speed_bin, y = fct_rev(equipment_ID), fill = pct_time)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white", linewidth = 0.4) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::label_comma(),
                     breaks = seq(0, 7000, by = 1000)) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "#eaf2f8", high = "#1d6fa4",
                      labels = scales::percent, name = "Share\nof time") +
  labs(x = "Speed setpoint (pkg/h, rounded to 500)", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
The speed regimes don’t overlap. Some machines run at high throughput; others at much lower setpoints. They don’t run at the same speed.
And their co-activity confirms the same thing:
#| fig-cap: "Fraction of total time where both machines are simultaneously in production. Dark = often together; light = rarely together."
#| fig-height: 3.5

coact <- coactivity_matrix(df, state = "production", res_min = 5)

bind_rows(
  coact,
  coact |> rename(machine_a = machine_b, machine_b = machine_a)
) |>
  bind_rows(
    tibble(
      machine_a = sort(unique(df$equipment_ID)),
      machine_b = sort(unique(df$equipment_ID)),
      co_active_pct = NA_real_, jaccard = NA_real_
    )
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(machine_a, machine_b, fill = co_active_pct)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white", linewidth = 0.6) +
  geom_text(
    aes(label = if_else(is.na(co_active_pct), "—",
                        scales::percent(co_active_pct, accuracy = 1))),
    size = 3.5, colour = "grey20", fontface = "bold"
  ) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "#eaf2f8", high = "#1d6fa4",
                      labels = scales::percent, na.value = "grey85",
                      name = "Co-activity") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank())






How to read this matrix





Each cell shows the fraction of total time where both machines are simultaneously in production (5-minute grid over the full history). A score near zero means they almost never run together — they alternate. A high score means they operate in parallel.



Some pairs run together. Others almost never do. Comparing their performance as if they were doing the same job would give us numbers that mean nothing.

title: When Machines Talk
text:
What the machines are hiding
No diagnosis yet. But we now have a map of what we don’t know.
133 alarm codes with no dictionary. A state — performance_loss — that slips through standard reporting. Counters that drift. Five machines that aren’t in the same league.

title: When Machines Talk
text:
What to do about it
These five machines can’t be pooled. Different speed regimes, different histories, different co-activity patterns. Aggregating them would give us averages that describe none of them.
The counters are unreliable at interval level. pi and po are useful over full days or longer. Below that, they measure noise.
performance_loss matters. It accounts for 28% of intervals. If we only look at downtimes, we miss a quarter of what’s going on.

Next: Let’s compute OEE. The results are not what the availability numbers would suggest.
